title: BYD files six more solid-state battery patents - electrive.com
content:
BYD has published six new patents covering key aspects of solid-state battery technology. The filings focus on improving the contact between electrodes and solid electrolytes as the company reportedly targets pilot production of dual-electrolyte cells in 2027.
Archive image: BYD's second-generation Blade Battery
Image: BYD
Four of the new patents concentrate on materials and cell chemistry. One proposes adding an ion-conducting, electrochemically stable interlayer between halide and sulphide electrolytes to prevent unwanted chemical reactions and extend cycle life. Another uses a first solid electrolyte as a buffer layer between the active cathode material and a sulphide electrolyte, aiming to improve stability while limiting heat generation. According to the patent, the active cathode layer should not release more than 117 joules per gram under thermal conditions.
Two further patents focus on the cathode structure itself. One describes a dual-layer composite cathode that combines monocrystalline and polycrystalline cathode materials with different solid electrolytes. BYD says the design seeks to combine the higher structural stability of monocrystalline materials with the superior rate performance of polycrystalline materials.
Another patent proposes a cathode based on three materials, in which lithiated metal oxides and metal sulphides are mixed with a solid electrolyte to reduce interfacial resistance, improve specific capacity and extend cycle life.
The remaining two patents move beyond materials science and towards manufacturing. One introduces ionic liquid wetting agents with a gradient distribution across the electrode to improve ion transport and maintain reliable contact between solid materials. The other defines a quality metric called ‘Re’ for the contact ratio between cathode and electrolyte particles. BYD states that at least 60 per cent of a cathode particle’s perimeter should be in contact with electrolyte particles to improve charging performance, capacity and durability.
The latest patents follow
a solid-state battery patent granted by the China National Intellectual Property Administration (CNIPA) in late July
covering composite cathode structures. According to Chinese media, BYD plans to start small-scale production of solid-state cells using its dual-electrolyte cathode design in 2027. The first cells are expected to be evaluated in prototype vehicles before any wider deployment. BYD has not officially confirmed the reported production timeline.
These new reports build on the company’s previously disclosed solid-state battery roadmap. Last year, BYD
confirmed it had already produced its first solid-state battery cells
and planned demonstration vehicles from 2027 before targeting broader commercialisation towards the end of the decade. Earlier this year, the manufacturer also
revealed progress in both sodium-ion and solid-state battery research
, underlining its strategy of developing multiple next-generation battery chemistries in parallel.
While BYD continues to advance the technology, large-scale production remains a challenge across the industry. In June, CATL Chairman Robin Zeng cautioned that engineering and manufacturing constraints mean
solid-state batteries are still several years away from mass-market deployment
. Nevertheless, the technology remains a major focus for battery manufacturers.

title: CATL Expands Its Lead in the Global Battery Market - electrive.com
content:
The global market for batteries used in electric and hybrid vehicles grew by 20 per cent in the first half of 2026. CATL increased its market share to around 40 per cent.
Third generation of the Shenxing battery from CATL
Image: CATL
According to the latest analysis by South Korean market research firm SNE Research, global EV battery cell demand reached 608.5 GWh in the first half of 2026, up 20 per cent year on year. However, growth slowed compared to
the full year 2025
, when demand increased by 31.7 per cent. The analysis covers battery cells used in battery-electric vehicles, plug-in hybrids and conventional hybrids.
CATL remained the market leader, with battery cell deliveries totalling 242.7 GWh in the first half of the year. The Chinese manufacturer increased deliveries by 25.3 per cent year on year, lifting its global market share from 38.2 to 39.9 per cent.
BYD remained in second place with battery cell deliveries of 87.7 GWh. However, its deliveries grew by just 1.6 per cent year on year, leaving it with a global market share of 14.4 per cent. Together, CATL and BYD accounted for 54.3 per cent of the global market for batteries used in electric and hybrid vehicles.
LG Energy Solution was the highest-ranked South Korean battery maker in third place. The company delivered 52.6 GWh in the first half of 2026, up 8.4 per cent year on year. However, its global market share fell from 9.6 to 8.6 per cent.
The top 10 battery suppliers for electric and hybrid vehicles in the first half of 2026 comprised seven Chinese manufacturers – CATL, BYD, CALB, Gotion, EVE, SVOLT and Sunwoda – alongside South Korea’s LG Energy Solution and SK On, and Japan’s Panasonic.

title: Amara Raja planning for new lead battery tech to aid sustainability – Batteries International
content:
Lead, News, Recycling
Read Later
Jayadev Galla, Amara Raja's chairman, MD and CEO, heads dedicated business responsibility leadership team
India’s Amara Raja Energy & Mobility has said it continues to make strides in boosting sustainable operations across the business — and plans investment in new lead battery tech processes and energy efficiencies.
The lead acid manufacturing major has set a target of restricting the group’s increase in carbon intensity (Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions) to 3% in fiscal year 2027, ending in March 2027, with planned energy efficiency projects and increased use of renewable energy.
Amara Raja revealed its commitments in its latest ‘Business responsibility and sustainability report’, released toward the end of July 2026.
The company, which is also venturing into the lithium battery sector, said it had used recycled lead for more than 88% of all lead and lead alloys consumed over the past year.
Recycled polypropylene copolymer (PC) — used in battery casings, covers and containers — was used for more than 8% of the total PC consumed during the year. Intensity of water usage was reduced by 7%, just missing the target of 8%.
During the reporting period, the company said its 67MW of installed renewable energy capacity helped avoid around 74,000 tonnes of CO₂ emissions.
Meanwhile, safety and employee well-being “remained non-negotiable priorities”. The company said it maintained zero fatalities across operations and continued strengthening its safety culture. A ‘Vitality Index Program’ was launched during the year covering annual medical examinations for almost all employees.
Looking ahead, Amara Raja said its future plan of action includes developing next-generation UPS battery technologies to strengthen its presence in international markets.
There will also be continued in-house and collaborative R&D initiatives on advanced lead acid and alternate battery chemistries, while developing advanced battery technologies for marine applications.
Amara Raja also intends to enhance plate quality through improved plate-making and advanced paste-mixing processes for automotive and UPS batteries, improving throughput and energy efficiency by optimising oven cycle times and assembly operations.
The group said it was determined to push ahead with moves to boost sustainable business operations, but warned it is battling the impact of geopolitical tensions, trade restrictions, logistics disruption and volatility in global commodity markets.
Wider economic turmoil may impact availability and pricing of key raw materials such as lead and other battery components, affecting operational continuity and costs in the lead acid battery business, Amara Raja said.
However, the group is diversifying its supplier base, increasing local sourcing and strengthening recycling in a bid to offset the impact.

reported
in June 2026 that Amara Raja is now largely ‘going it alone’ on LFP cells development after a flagship licensing tech partnership with a Chinese supplier came under pressure from Beijing.

title: Viridi BESS selected for Oak Ridge Lab grid research partnership – Batteries International
content:
Energy Storage, Lithium, News
Read Later
Viridi's RPS 150 BESS installed at ORNL's Power Distribution Field Test Site
US BESS developer Viridi has announced a partnership with Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) to support research into next-generation utility grid technologies.
As part of the partnership, announced on July 28, Viridi installed its lithium ion-based RPS 150 BESS at ORNL’s Grid Research Innovation and Development Center (GRID-C) as part of the testing platform for a Department of Energy resource integration and evaluation project.
Viridi said the research began with ORNL developing a system for controlling clusters of grid resources to meet utility needs.
The developed technology was first tested in an indoor laboratory using emulated energy sources and battery storage — and followed up with testing in a live grid with real resources to correct any issues emerging from complex equipment interactions and real-world battery charging dynamics.
ORNL integrated its converter system with Viridi’s battery to validate the technology. Testing has now concluded and ORNL is expected to present the project’s findings in the coming months.
Viridi said its trailer-BESS design is suitable for off-grid power supply, grid reinforcement, emergency backup and renewable energy self-consumption from sources like wind and solar.
Battery packs incorporate advanced fire suppression and pioneering anti-propagation technology. Viridi said its proprietary design isolates each cell to prevent thermal runaway, ensuring that a single failure does not escalate.
“Being selected by ORNL to support the project is a milestone for Viridi and a validation of what we have built,” said Viridi CEO Jon Williams.
“We built Viridi’s fail-safe BESS to perform in exactly these kinds of environments, and we are proud to be partnering with ORNL to advance the grid modernisation solutions that utilities across the country need.”

title: SK On, Factorial join forces for solid-state EV batteries plan – Batteries International
content: SK On and Factorial Energy have launched a new alliance aimed at driving solid-state EV battery tech from labs to production lines. The partnership, announced on July 29, brings together US-based Factorial’s advanced cell technology and scale-up expertise with the South Korean battery maker’s global manufacturing base network and pilot capabilities. A key objective of a memorandum of understanding between the firms is to assess whether and how SK On’s lithium ion manufacturing network could support future development of solid-state battery technologies. SK On, a subsidiary of SK Innovation, will jointly evaluate the technical feasibility and manufacturing considerations for Factorial’s FEST solid-state battery tech. Factorial said the move highlights its “capital-light approach” to industrialisation, which is centered on developing batteries that can use established manufacturing infrastructure to accelerate the path to commercialisation. “A battery breakthrough only matters if it can be manufactured at scale,” said Siyu Huang, CEO of Factorial. Head of the Institute of Future Technology at SK On, Ki-soo Park, said the collaboration will consider opportunities to support the future development of solid-state battery technologies for mobility and high-performance markets. In 2024, auto giant Stellantis said it was introducing a demonstration fleet of EVs fitted with solid-state batteries from Factorial. title: WaveTech plans battery tech hub for Norway energy cluster partnership – Batteries International
content: WaveTech is to establish a ‘battery rejuvenation hub’ in Norway, as the latest member of national energy organisation Energy Transition Norway (ETN). ETN, which connects operators, suppliers, investors, research institutions and others in the energy sector, said technology developed by WaveTech recovers lost capacity and extends the useful life of batteries, rather than replacing them too early. WaveTech’s innovative Crystal Control Technology (CCT) has been developed to boost performance, enhance capacity and increase energy output of lead and lithium batteries. The battery tech firm confirmed on July 10 it had joined ETN, with the ambition of setting up a hub in Stavanger “as a natural starting point”. WaveTech works primarily with businesses for which batteries are critical to operations, including telecoms, data centres, energy storage, UPS and the wider industrial sector. The company said its approach is based on more than 20 years of research in electrochemistry. This research underpins methods and systems that allow the company to assess what a battery is actually capable of, recover lost capacity, and extend its usable life. WaveTech cited what it said was a recent 90-day pilot with an unnamed global provider of UPS, in which WaveTech recovered capacity in 2,624 of 3,056 batteries that would otherwise have been sent for recycling. In a similar project involving typical telecom batteries from a recycling facility, over 70% of the batteries tested proved suitable for capacity recovery, the firm said. ETN spokesperson Mariia Bartakhanova said: “The aim is to help these organisations get more out of the batteries they already have — for longer, and with a meaningful environmental benefit.” Batteries International reported in 2023 that WaveTech’s German subsidiary was testing CCT on a combination of lead batteries and solar power providing backup power for telecoms systems in Indonesia. That project followed WaveTech’s successful completion of the first commercial installation of CCT in Malaysia with Maxis Telecommunications. In 2024, Norway, a non-EU member state, agreed to cooperate with the bloc in  developing raw materials for Europe’s battery industry. title: Rombat’s legal fight over EU price-fixing fine ‘to take two years’ – Batteries International
content: Lead battery manufacturer Rombat’s legal tussle over a fine for breaching EU antitrust rules is set to drag on for up to two years, the firm’s parent company has revealed. South Africa’s Metair Investments launched an appeal over Rombat’s €20.2 million ($24 million) fine from the European Commission last March. However, Metair warned on August 3 that the legal battle could drag on for two years before the case is finalised. Metair also said a financial guarantee, as security for the first instalment of the fine, is being provided following an interim hearing last month at the General Court — the lower court of the Court of Justice of the European Union, handling cases brought by individuals, companies, and member states against EU institutions. In December 2025, the European Commission named several manufacturers, including Rombat, it said had entered into “anticompetitive agreements and engaged in concerted practices related to the sale of automotive starter batteries to automotive original equipment manufacturers in the European Economic Area” for more than 12 years. Fines totalling around €72 million were issued, including those for Exide and FET (including its predecessor Elettra), together with trade association EUROBAT. Clarios (formerly JC Autobatterie), was also named, but not fined, because it received full immunity for revealing the existence of the cartel. The Commission said that as lead was the most important input material and cost factor for the batteries concerned, battery producers paid a premium to suppliers to procure lead with the necessary quality. “This cartel restricted competition and may have led to higher prices for the manufacturing of cars and trucks in Europe.” The post Rombat’s legal fight over EU price-fixing fine ‘to take two years’ appeared first on Batteries International .

title: Ford Fathom Electric Pickup Starts at $29,945
content:

The automaker's new battery-electric truck matches Maverick hybrid pricing while offering compact SUV interior room & hands-free driving.
August 6, 2026

The name of Ford's upcoming mid-size EV pickup truck.
Ford Motor Co.
At a Glance
Starting price of $29,945 includes destination charges, matching Ford's Maverick hybrid pickup.
Interior space exceeds Toyota RAV4 compact SUV with frunk and bi-directional charging included.
BlueCruise hands-free driver assistance available via subscription on all Fathom models.
Ford has continued the slow drip of news for its upcoming
low-priced battery-electric pickup truck
, with the announcement of the name Fathom and the starting price of $29,945, including destination charges. That’s almost exactly the same as the company’s
Maverick mid-sized hybrid-electric pickup
, for comparison.
Pre-ordering will open early next year, and Ford has revealed that the Fathom will have more interior space than a Toyota RAV4 compact SUV. There is an Apple CarPlay/Android Auto-supporting touch screen infotainment system (in contrast to the bring-your-own-device philosophy of would-be rival Slate), a frunk, and bi-directional charging capability.
Ford has not yet announced a switch from the costly DC bi-directional charging seen in the
F-150 Lightning
that necessitates a costly home inverter to the more affordable AC bi-directional charging that does not, but it would be in keeping with the Fathom’s cost-effective approach.
Additionally, every Fathom will be able to employ Ford’s subscription-based BlueCruise hands-free driver assistance system.
Kay Hart, general manager for Ford’s Model e electrification effort, says that the company “scoured the Ford archives, looking at how this company has named vehicles for more than a century.”
But after naming the current hybrid-electric mid-size pickup after Ford’s second-generation compact sedan, the Maverick, the company passed over the name from its original compact sedan, the Falcon, in favor of Fathom. This name communicates the notion of depth below the surface, according to Hart.
Prospective buyers will probably be more concerned with the price of options and Fathom’s capabilities than the truck’s name. We’ll find out in 2027, when Ford starts delivering them.

title: Why innocent drinks is Prioritising Supply Chain Resilience
content:
Why innocent drinks is Prioritising Supply Chain Resilience
Prioritise Us
on Google
Innocent has announced the winners of the 2026 Farmer Innovation Fund. Credit: Innocent
innocent drinks has announced 18 projects which are increasing resilience across fruit and vegetable supply chains, looking at AI and sustainability
As supply chains around the world become more complex, the fruit and veg one is particularly vulnerable.
Ongoing climate events have made the environment unstable, resulting in high temperatures, droughts, forest fires and flash foods – all of which are making fresh food supply chains unstable.
innocent drinks is working to mitigate vulnerabilities, having conducted its fifth Farmer Innovation Fund and announcing 10 winners, with 18 projects, all working towards
building greater resilience
in the fruit and veg supply chain.
The resilience of our supply chain starts with the resilience of the farms we source from.
Mario Diaz Marcos, Sustainability & Climate Resilience Lead at Innocent drinks
A growing concern
Recent years have introduced a series of risks for supply chains, uncovering vulnerabilities that have previously gone unnoticed. Floods, fires and droughts have all put pressure on food production, but so has the increasing population and the growing awareness of sustainability.
Now, governments around the world are prioritising food security as a national issue, with an ongoing need to collaborate with farmers and suppliers. Regenerative agriculture and traceability programmes have become key to developing
resilience in fruit and vegetable
supply chains.
Coca-Cola-owned company innocent drinks produces smoothies and drinks which are sold across supermarkets, cafes and other outlets. It started doing business in 1999, with a commitment of responsible production. The ethos of the company is based on leaving things better than they were found, with the planet at a core part of everything it does.
In 2021, innocent drinks set up the Farmer Innovation Fund, an annual pot of money which helps its suppliers grow fruit and veg long into the future. It is a £1m (US$1.3m) programme which aims to support farmers and suppliers as they adopt climate-resilient practises, like
regenerative agriculture
innocent has now announced the winners of this year's fund, with a collection of 10 winners, spanning across 14 countries and 18 projects.
"Being able to bring fruit and veg to more people, starts entirely with the people who grow it," explains Nick Canney, CEO at innocent drinks.
Innocent is committed to driving resilience. Credit: Innocent
"This year's winners are taking on some of the biggest challenges facing agriculture today, from climate resilience and water management to carbon reduction and biodiversity. We're delighted to support these innovative projects and look forward to seeing the positive impact they can deliver.”
Winning projects
More than half of innocent's carbon footprint comes from its ingredients, which means the FIF is the brand's biggest opportunity to tackle scope 3 emissions. The winning projects are operating across four continents, focusing on eight core ingredients necessary within innocent's supply chain, including oranges, apples, coconuts, grapes, strawberries and mangoes.
“Oranges are a strategically important ingredient, and building resilient citrus supply chains starts with understanding the real impact of actions taken on the farm," explains Garett Stoll, Senior Consultant, at 3Keel.
Garett Stoll, Senior Consultant, at 3Keel
"Through this pilot, we're testing a rigorous new approach to measuring greenhouse gas emissions and carbon removals, combining farm data, soil sampling and remote sensing to generate credible, science-based insights. Our ambition is to create a scalable framework that can help strengthen climate reporting, support growers and unlock greater confidence in the role agriculture can play in tackling climate change.”
The projects are using significant innovations in order to support farmers around the world, whether tackling citrus diseases in Brazil, or supporting coconut farmers in the Philippines.
In Brazil, one project is prioritising citrus supply chains, measuring greenhouse gas emissions and carbon removals at farm level. Using a SAI Platforms's Farm Sustainability Assessment citrus farm, the project will use remote sensing, soil sampling, farm data and carbon modelling. This will help with measuring, reporting and verification. Once the pilot is complete, this could be utilised across global supply chains, helping increase climate smart farming practises.
One winner, SVZ, is increasing efficiency and sustainability in
strawberry production,
using AI-powered decisions. These help growers optimise irrigation, through the combination of soil moisture, weather, crop and satellite data.
"The resilience of our supply chain starts with the resilience of the farms we source from," Mario Diaz Marcos, Sustainability & Climate Resilience Lead at Innocent drinks, explains to Supply Chain Digital.
Mario Diaz Marcos, Sustainability & Climate Resilience Lead at Innocent drinks
"Through the Farmer Innovation Fund, we're investing in projects that help farmers adapt to climate challenges, protect key ingredients and secure long-term supply. The insights from these
initiatives
will help us better understand what works on the ground and support more resilient fruit and veg supply chains for the future."
Meeting demand
Changing consumer demand has also had an impact on food and drink supply chains – the growing popularity of coconut water has driven the need for resilient production. Partnerships with Peter Paul,  the world's largest integrated coconut processor, is therefore critical in developing
sustainable farming
practises which encourage resilience and long-term stability.
"Our project helps farmers in the Bondoc Peninsula and Pagbilao clusters with mulching techniques to improve soil moisture, fertility and yield. By strengthening resilience at the farm level, we can help farming communities better adapt to the increasing impacts of climate change," explains Clarito Q. Ona, Fair Trade Officer at Peter Paul Philippine Corporation.
Five winners from this year have been previous winners of the fund, demonstrating the commitment of investing in long-term partnerships. innocent is demonstrating how to build scalable and resilient food supply chain strategies.

title: SE Advisory Services & IESE on Supply Chain Decarbonisation
content:
SE Advisory Services & IESE on Supply Chain Decarbonisation
Prioritise Us
on Google
"Sustainability goes far beyond compliance," says SE Advisory. Credit: Getty
SE Advisory Services and IESE explore how sustainability in supply chains is still an aim instead of a reality, examining barriers to implementation
Supply chains contain the largest share of both environmental exposure and potential value creation for corporations, sitting outside their immediate operational footprint.
According to the 2026 Executive Report by SE Advisory Services and IESE Business School, this external concentration makes procurement and traceability critical to long-term enterprise value.
Scope 3 emissions
account for more than 70% of total corporate emissions on average, according to the report. This makes supply chain monitoring an operational necessity rather than a reporting exercise.
Climate Risk Is No Longer a Future Problem
Procurement and climate exposure
Climate hazards could erode up to 7% of annual corporate earnings by 2035, according to World Economic Forum estimates. This makes climate-related asset exposure a core determinant of valuation, earnings volatility and enterprise value.
For the world's largest companies, the projected annual financial impact of climate physical risk could reach up to US$1.2tn in coming decades, according to SE Advisory Services and IESE Business School. This figure does not account for second-order impacts on revenue, demand or
supply chain disruption
The report shows that only 35% of companies have context-specific climate adaptation plans in place and only 30% report on them.
Sustainable procurement
programmes can help to mitigate these risks. According to the report, approximately one-third of companies report such initiatives have successfully prevented supply chain disruptions.
Circular models and material flows
Strategic practices like circular procurement and the reintegration of secondary raw materials could reduce energy intensity and input costs while bolstering supply security, according to the report. One industrial group's move to circular business models was modelled to add €1bn (US$1.14bn) in incremental revenue.
"In one industrial company's shift to a circular business model, the opportunity was modelled to generate €1bn (US$1.14bn) in incremental revenue," writes Steve Wilhite, Executive Vice President at SE Advisory Services, on LinkedIn.
Steve Wilhite, Executive Vice President, SE Advisory Services
Steve notes that companies with financial discipline report up to 20% lower energy use in the first year and up to 30% less unplanned downtime.
"The upside can extend well beyond operational savings," writes Steve.
Deploying digital traceability platforms allows organisations to move from estimated supplier data to verified figures. This could capture new commercial opportunities and strengthen margin resilience.
Data infrastructure and verification
The report concludes that capturing the full upside of sustainability relies on what SE Advisory Services and IESE Business School term the Capability Multiplier. Value is realised only when measurement, governance and digital execution align.
Integrated digital capability could reduce the time required to collect and validate ESG data by 25% to 40%, according to the report. Deploying digital monitoring tools alongside governance controls could help companies achieve up to 20% lower energy use in their first year and up to 30% less unplanned downtime.
"One idea from this research stayed with me. Yes, sustainability creates value. But this value capture doesn't happen automatically," writes Steve on LinkedIn. "A surprising amount of sustainability value never reaches the bottom line."
SE Advisory aims to minimise risk while boosting innovation amid climate shifts. Credit: SE Advsisory
Industrial energy use presents the most immediate financial return when evaluated with a holistic strategic approach, according to the report. Energy efficiency functions as a direct margin and resilience strategy, protecting operations against volatile input costs.
Studies cited in the report show variations in energy consumption
across manufacturing
sites producing identical goods. These include a five-fold gap in plastic bag manufacturing and a seven-fold gap in brick production.
When companies evaluate efficiency projects, including operational benefits like reduced downtime and lower maintenance alongside raw energy savings, the total value of the initiative increases by 40% to 250%, according to the report. Within industrial energy projects, targeted efficiency optimisation initiatives typically deliver 15% to 20% in energy savings with payback periods of three to four years.
In access to capital, a single decarbonisation roadmap unlocked roughly €100m (US$113m) in sustainability-linked financing.
Changing strategies
Sustainability performance has shifted from a reputational signal into a direct input for credit risk assessments and capital allocation, the report says. Companies with credible, integrated sustainability strategies benefit from improved risk perceptions, stronger investor confidence and measurably lower borrowing costs.
Across European capital markets, more than 75% of investors report sustainability performance shapes their allocation decisions. Private markets and equity investors increasingly reward deeply embedded sustainability business models with higher valuation multiples.
Integrated
decarbonisation roadmaps
directly unlock capital. Verified ESG credentials enabled a global manufacturer to secure up to €100m (US$113m) in sustainability-linked financing.
The report concludes that treating sustainability as a measurable performance lever allows companies to protect earnings stability while improving access to competitive financing. Effective governance requires connecting sustainability metrics directly to capital allocation,
board oversight
and executive incentives.
Modern corporate strategy involves framing sustainability as a financial performance factor rather than a compliance function. Although most large organisations possess high ambition and vast data, a large portion of potential financial value is left uncaptured due to a gap in organisational capability.
The CXO Summit

PG Consulting is making significant waves with its expansion into Europe. What was the strategic catalyst behind consolidating your operations in the region and choosing Lisbon as your hub?

European

strategy

That is our "Executive Pedigree" pillar. Our team is composed entirely of former executives from giants like AB InBev, Coca-Cola, P&G and Kraft Heinz. When a client faces a

title: Amazon Business: Optimising Inventory With Machine Learning
content:
Amazon Business: Optimising Inventory With Machine Learning
Prioritise Us
on Google
Intelligent Inventory Optimisation With Machine Learning
Machine learning and automated replenishment systems transform how modern businesses manage inventory during persistent global supply chain disruption
Balancing inventory remains one of the most complex areas of supply chain operations. Organisations must maintain product availability while controlling costs, reducing excess stock and responding to changing customer demand.
The challenge has intensified as disruption and fragmented global supply networks make inventory decisions more dynamic than traditional models can handle. Businesses face pressure to operate more efficiently without compromising service levels or resilience.
Inventory optimisation now requires a more responsive approach. Machine learning is reshaping how organisations analyse large volumes of data in real time, detect patterns earlier and anticipate fluctuations more accurately. These technologies enable businesses to move beyond reactive planning towards predictive strategies that account for multiple variables simultaneously.
In a recent webinar with Marc Malone, Project Executive, Offering Manager at
Consulting and Rick McDonald, Former Chief Supply Chain Officer at the
Company, the two discuss the future of intelligent inventory optimisation with machine learning.
Watch the full webinar
Intelligent Inventory Optimisation With Machine Learning
on-demand now.
Rick McDonald, Former Chief Supply Chain Officer at the Clorox Company
Growing unpredictability across supply and demand cycles
"We're in a period of permanent
disruption
," says Rick. "The pressure is even greater on supply chain leaders with respect to customer service, margin expansion, growth and balance sheet optimisation."
Supply chains were once more stable and predictable. Demand patterns were consistent, lead times were reliable and planning cycles were longer. Organisations could rely on established processes and historical precedents to guide decision-making.
"You could build a forecast based on historical data; that'd be good enough," says Marc. "That's no longer the case, because of a couple of factors – one is demand volatility; buying behaviours shift quickly, that's based on economic uncertainty, digital commerce and changing customer expectations. Therefore, historical data is less reliable than it used to be."
Marc Malone, Project Executive, Offering Manager at IBM Consulting
​​​​​​Marc adds that supply chain
disruptions
create an environment that is less stable than even five years ago. Longer and more variable lead times, supplier instability and geopolitical pressures all create uncertainty on the supply side. These compounding factors mean organisations must continuously reassess their inventory positions.
The two concluded that while the challenge remains the same, the environment demands faster solutions that can adapt to changing conditions in real time.
"These challenges can be addressed by AI," says Marc. "Specifically, machine learning can provide autonomous replenishment and better demand forecasting."
Three areas where legacy planning falls short:
Prior demand forecasts were backwards-looking — traditional forecasts relied primarily on historical data, but with changing demand and various factors, that's a less reliable way to forecast what's happening in the future.
Slow to adapt — legacy planning solutions operate on a weekly or monthly cycle, and in today's environment, conditions can change within a few days, so organisations using legacy systems are always one step behind.
Inability to self-correct — legacy systems operate as one-directional, static forecasts, without a mechanism to learn from new information or changing conditions.
Legacy planning approaches face limits
Planning methods were designed for a more stable world. That world no longer exists. Traditional systems struggle to incorporate the volume and variety of data now available, leaving organisations vulnerable to unexpected shifts.
"One of the best I've seen is Kinaxis. They have something called a polymathic solver that runs in the background to continuously scan the environment, both the structured data a company has and all the unstructured data that might affect how the forecast is going to change," says Rick.
Marc says that IBM has proprietary solutions that take advantage of end-to-end supply chain visibility. The systems take into account various macro and micro conditions, then use
algorithms and machine learning to deliver results that surpass human analytical capabilities.
"At IBM, we have proprietary solutions that take advantage of exactly that: looking at the end-to-end supply chain, taking into account all the various macro and micro conditions affecting it, and then, with AI algorithms and
machine learning
, delivering a far more accurate result than any human could achieve on their own. That's what's exciting about it," says Marc.

title: Tesla admits Cybertruck PCS defect, extends warranty to 8 years
content:
Tesla has officially acknowledged that the power conversion system (PCS) in pre-2026 Cybertrucks is defective, and it’s extending the warranty on those trucks to 8 years or 150,000 miles.
The reversal comes after months of owners paying up to $7,200 to replace a part Tesla now admits “does not meet our reliability standards.” The automaker sneakily tried to let the clear manufacturing defect pass warranties.
What Tesla is finally doing
In a statement posted to its official Cybertruck account, Tesla said it “identified PCS electronics in pre-2026 Cybertrucks that do not meet our reliability standards and have made design changes to address this in newer vehicles.”
That’s the admission owners had been waiting for. It came with a list of fixes.
Pre-2026 trucks, meaning the 2024 and 2025 Foundation Series and standard builds, get their PCS coverage extended to 8 years or 150,000 miles, which basically means it’s now part of the powertrain warranty rather than the overall warranty.
The 2026 Cybertruck, which already ships with a redesigned PCS, carries a shorter 7-year/70,000-mile warranty on the part. Owners who already paid out of pocket will be reimbursed in the coming weeks. And a software update now lets the truck Supercharge even when the PCS has failed, so a dead unit no longer strands the vehicle. Tesla says it’s also covering Supercharging for affected owners until it clears the parts backlog.
The warranty math is the whole story
We reported in July that the PCS failures were starting to be widespread. A self-selected owner poll showed 91 of 223 Cybertrucks, nearly 41%, had needed a PCS replacement, with new failures logged every week. The part combines the onboard charger and the DC-DC converter, so when it dies, home charging drops from 48 amps to 24 and then quits entirely.
Here’s the problem. The 2024 and 2025 trucks shipped with Tesla’s basic 4-year/50,000-mile warranty, and the PCS wasn’t singled out for anything longer. A unit that failed outside that window left the owner with a $5,000 to $7,200 bill. Tesla had quietly been discounting the repair to around $1,000 as a “goodwill” gesture, which, as we said at the time, was the company all but admitting the part was defective.
Now it’s saying so out loud, and moving the coverage to 8 years. For a defect hitting 40% of trucks, that’s the difference between a manageable problem and a $7,000 gut punch.
Tesla has run this play before. It extended warranties on the eMMC memory failures in its older touchscreens back in 2020, but only after NHTSA opened an investigation. Other automakers do it too. Hyundai and Kia extended warranties over their ICCU failures earlier this year. And Tesla has recalled Cybertrucks before to replace faulty inverters.
Electrek’s Take
Credit where it’s due: this is the right outcome. An 8-year/150,000-mile warranty, reimbursements for owners who already paid, and a software fix so a failed PCS doesn’t kill charging entirely. That’s what taking responsibility for a manufacturing defect is supposed to look like.
Top comment by Henry
🚗 The REAL bummer here is Tesla refuses to replace my PCS at 42,000mi on Model Y LR 2020 that they KNOW is defective for $3,765!! There was a prior recall on these defective PCS parts for Model 3's and even though my car was built with one -- NHTSA did not include my model year.
Clearly the PCS is a big problem for ALL Tesla customers -- it's a question of when not if yours will fail out of warranty.🚕🚧🚧
I even filed a NHTSA complaint and nothing. The Tesla service centers in Irvine and Aliso Viejo, ca were very nasty about it and refused any goodwill assistance. So now I get to wait and see when my 12v battery starts dying since the PCS charges that too!
But it’s a bummer it took this long, and it took pressure to get here. Owners were eating $7,000 repair bills while Tesla’s first instinct was a quiet $1,000 discount instead of an admission before we reported on the issue.
It took the owner forums, our reporting, and other outlets hammering on this for weeks before Tesla put its name to the problem. Doing the right thing only after you’re pushed into it isn’t quite the same as doing the right thing.
And that’s the pattern worth watching. There’s a real tendency here to let a clear manufacturing defect run past a short warranty and make the customer eat the cost. A part that fails on 40% of trucks isn’t a fluke. It’s a defect, and Tesla knew it well before this statement. The warranty extension is welcome. The instinct to see how many owners would just pay up first is not. We’ll be watching whether the reimbursements actually land, and whether it takes a failure rate this high, or an NHTSA nudge, to get the same result next time.

title: Telo raises its tiny electric truck's tow rating to 8,000 lbs
content:
TELO Trucks
Fred Lambert
| Aug 7 2026 - 7:06 am PT
Telo is raising the tow rating on its Mini-sized electric truck to 8,000 lbs, up from the 6,600 lbs it previously advertised.
The startup says months of real-world towing convinced it the little MT1 can safely pull more than a truck that size looks like it should. That new number puts a 152-inch pickup roughly on par with a base Ford F-150.
Co-founder and CTO Forest North announced the change in a video, framing it around his own needs. “In the beginning, we set a stake in the ground that we wanted to be able to tow over 6,000 pounds. I personally have a travel trailer and I wanted to make sure that I could tow that,” he said. “Now that we’re further into it, we have towed a bunch of things. We understand towing and what this vehicle can do.”
The MT1 is about as small as a modern pickup gets. At 152 inches long, it’s the size of an electric Mini Cooper, yet it carries a full 60-to-96-inch bed and seats up to five. It runs a dual-motor all-wheel-drive setup rated at 500 hp, with a 77 kWh standard pack good for 260 miles or a 106 kWh long-range pack rated at 350-plus miles. Telo starts it at $41,520 and is targeting first deliveries in late 2026.
Why Telo thinks a small truck can tow big
North’s argument leans on the physics that favor an electric drivetrain when there’s a trailer on the hitch.
The first is braking. A four-wheel-drive electric truck that can move a lot of power in and out of its pack can regen down a long grade almost indefinitely, he argues, instead of cooking its brakes. “That means that we can regen for miles and miles and miles going down a pass — you’re not touching your brakes and yet you have complete control over your vehicle and your trailer,” North said.
Heat is the other half of it. Combustion trucks dump most of their energy as heat and then have to shed even more of it under load, which is exactly what SAE’s J2807 tow standard is built to stress with tests like the 11-mile, 6% Davis Dam grade run. North says that math barely applies to an EV: “For us, it really doesn’t change the equation that much. We have so much torque and so much horsepower together, and it’s instant. That makes starting on a grade so easy.”
Then there’s the packaging. The MT1’s hitch sits close to the rear axle, giving a shorter lever arm so trailer tongue weight doesn’t lift the front end the way it would on a longer truck. And despite its footprint, the MT1 isn’t light — North puts it at over 4,000 lbs — riding on a steel chassis with a crossmember tying the hitch to the frame. Small, in his telling, is a structural advantage: the same strength takes less mass than it would on a full-size truck.
North was blunt about the limits. For long hauls, “a big diesel truck is probably going to be better for the near term.” The MT1’s pitch is shorter trips, where a compact, easy-to-park truck that tows well is more convenient than a full-size rig.
The 8,000-lb number unlocks a new class of trailer
The jump from 6,600 to 8,000 lbs isn’t a random bump. It’s aimed at a wave of trailers that carry their own batteries and motors.
Telo already showed this off in July, when
the MT1 towed Pebble’s 5,800-lb Flow electric travel trailer
. The Flow’s “Easy Tow” active propulsion system uses the trailer’s own drivetrain and regen to cut the effective load on the tow vehicle, which is how a truck the size of a Mini pulled a full-size camper without drama. North says a lot of these new powered trailers land in the 6,000-to-8,000-lb range, so the higher rating is what lets the MT1 be a real option for them.
That same electrical headroom is what makes the regen story credible. Telo
confirmed 400 kW sustained charging
for the MT1 in June, running a dual 800V/400V pack architecture. A truck that can absorb that many kilowatts on a charger can also absorb a lot of regen coming down a hill.
How 8,000 lbs stacks up against other trucks
Against full-size electric pickups, 8,000 lbs is on the low end. But the point isn’t the number on its own — it’s the number relative to the size of the truck.
Here’s where the MT1 lands:
Telo MT1 (152 in): 8,000 lbs
Ford F-150 Lightning: 10,000 lbs
Tesla Cybertruck: 11,000 lbs
Rivian R1T: 11,000 lbs
GMC Hummer EV pickup: 12,000 lbs
Chevy Silverado EV: 12,500 lbs
For gas comparison, a 2025 F-150 tows anywhere from about 8,400 lbs with the base 2.7L V6 up to 13,500 lbs fully optioned. So Telo’s tiny truck now claims to tow roughly what an entry-level full-size F-150 does, in a package nearly four feet shorter and thousands of pounds lighter. None of the full-size EV trucks come close to the MT1 on footprint or on the $41,520 starting price.
Electrek’s Take
This is impressive and exciting, but I still think it’s worth staying skeptical.
Telo has done a lot with very little. The company has raised roughly $20 million total — including a Series A
led by Tesla co-founder Marc Tarpenning
— and it’s trying to get to production readiness and pass federal requirements on that. In an industry where startups routinely burn through hundreds of millions before building a single sellable vehicle, that capital efficiency is genuinely notable. The towing physics North describes are real, too. Instant torque and heavy regen do make EVs good tow vehicles – albeit for shorter distances depending on the energy capacity.
But Telo is trying to build a Swiss army knife: a truck that’s tiny yet tows 8,000 lbs, charges at 400 kW, seats five, carries a Hummer-sized bed, and starts at $41,520. Each of those is a strong claim on its own. Stacking all of them into one production vehicle, and hitting every one consistently once real units are rolling off a line, is a much harder problem than showing it on a prototype. Tow ratings especially tend to get conservative once liability and warranty teams get involved.
And all of it still hangs on the biggest “if” of all: whether Telo actually reaches volume production. The prototype work is impressive. Deliveries are targeted for late 2026. We’ll see if the production truck can do everything the pre-production one promises.

title: Batch eFT.3 Review: A 28 MPH fat tire e-bike built for the streets
content:
Micah Toll
| Aug 7 2026 - 6:15 am PT
Fat tire e-bikes have become synonymous with rugged adventure. Browse the category and you’d think every 20-inch fat tire bike is destined for sandy beaches, forest trails, or rocky singletrack. In reality, though, most of them spend their lives on city streets, bike paths, and neighborhood roads.
That’s what makes the
Batch Bicycles eFT.3
refreshing. Instead of pretending to be an off-road machine, it embraces what many riders are actually looking for: a comfortable, practical commuter that happens to ride on fat tires.
The first clue is in the tires themselves.
While they’re the familiar 20×4-inch size, Batch skipped the aggressive knobby tread in favor of a smoother, commuter-oriented pattern.
Combined with a suspension fork and an included suspension seatpost, the setup is designed less for conquering trails and more for soaking up potholes, expansion joints, cracked pavement, and all the other imperfections that make urban riding uncomfortable.
Check them out in my video review below to see what I mean.
That philosophy of a road-focused commuter e-bike carries throughout the rest of the bike.
The eFT.3 arrives commuter-ready with full-coverage fenders, integrated front and rear LED lighting, and a sturdy rear rack. Those aren’t glamorous accessories, but they’re the kind of equipment that makes an e-bike more useful as a transportation tool.
Even riders who never intentionally venture out in the rain will appreciate fenders after rolling through a puddle or wet streets, and the rear rack means groceries or a work bag don’t have to live on your back.
Visually, the bike also stands out in a sea of matte black e-bikes. My test bike’s bright blue paint gives it plenty of personality without being flashy, and it’s a welcome change from the increasingly monochrome e-bike market.
I know they say that black is the best-selling bicycle color, but it’s just so boring. Give me colors, please!
Power comes from a 750W rear hub motor paired with a torque sensor, and it’s a combination that works well. The torque sensor gives pedal assist a much more natural feel than the cadence sensors found on many entry-level fat tire bikes, while the Class 3 setup provides pedal assist all the way to 28 mph (45 km/h).
The throttle is limited to 20 mph (32 km/h), as required for Class 2 e-bikes, but having that higher assisted top speed makes longer commutes feel much more practical.
The motor itself has no shortage of power. It accelerates confidently and never feels like it’s struggling.
There is one catch, however.
It’s loud.
Not just slightly louder than average, but noticeably so whenever you accelerate. Performance isn’t affected, and some riders won’t care, but if you’ve grown accustomed to the whisper-quiet motors appearing on many newer e-bikes, it’s something you’ll immediately notice.
A 48V, 15Ah LG battery provides 720 Wh of capacity, which is a healthy size for this category. As always, real-world range depends on speed, rider weight, terrain, and assist level, but it’s large enough that I never found myself worrying about making it home.
Component-wise, Batch seems to have made practical compromises .
The Shimano Tourney 7-speed drivetrain sits at the bottom of Shimano’s lineup, and no one is going to mistake it for premium equipment. Still, this isn’t a performance bike chasing lap times or trying to impress anyone with mid-shelf or top-shelf components. For commuting and everyday riding, it shifts reliably and gets the job done. It will probably require more frequent maintenance and you should avoid smacking it on any curbs, but it gets the job done.
The Tektro hydraulic disc brakes, on the other hand, punch above their weight. Equipped with 180 mm rotors, they offer confident stopping power with the predictable feel and lower maintenance that hydraulic systems are known for.
One design decision I particularly appreciated is something the bike
have: a folding frame.
Many 20-inch fat tire e-bikes include a folding mechanism
simply because that’s become the norm. But the reality is that plenty of owners never fold their bikes. In fact, there’s a good chance that the
majority
of folding e-bike owners never fold their bikes.
Overall, the eFT.3 feels like a company that understood its assignment. It isn’t trying to convince riders they’re buying an electric mountain bike simply because it has fat tires. Instead, it’s a comfortable, practical urban commuter that uses those oversized tires to improve ride quality rather than trail capability.
The loud motor is my biggest criticism, and at an
MSRP of $1,999
(currently discounted to
around $1,799
through September), it isn’t competing in the budget category. The Shimano Tourney drivetrain is also fairly basic, especially at that price point. But one could argue that those compromises are partially balanced by thoughtful commuter features, a large battery, hydraulic brakes, Class 3 performance, and a comfortable ride that feels purpose-built for everyday transportation.
If your riding consists primarily of pavement, bike paths, and city streets, and you appreciate the confidence and comfort that fat tires provide, the Batch Bicycles eFT.3 is well worth a closer look. It’s proof that not every fat tire e-bike needs to dream of mountain trails – sometimes the best adventure is simply making your daily ride more enjoyable.
